L01.title: Did the Model Change? Efficiently Assessing Machine Learning API Shifts

C4a.object: The year-over-year shift of a commercial classification API's confusion matrix (hard predicted labels) on a fixed labelled benchmark, estimated under a query budget by the MASA adaptive sampler with a 95%-confidence bound on its finite-sample estimation error.
C4a.quote: Since the data distribution remains ﬁxed, such a change is due to ML APIs’ updates.
C4a.reason: The same-weights floor is missing: the paper never re-queries the same API version on the same items to measure its own spread, attributes every change on the fixed set to the update and judges it against a bare 1% threshold, and its only interval (95% confidence of ≤1% Frobenius error) bounds MASA's sampling error in estimating ∆C rather than grading the shift against an in-situ spread; the object is hard-label confusion matrices, not log-probabilities.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Chen et al. 2021 grade an API's year-over-year confusion-matrix shift against a fixed 1% threshold, not a floor

bearing_quotes: For each dataset, we evaluated three commercial ML APIs’ accuracy in April 2020 and April 2021.
Since the data distribution remains ﬁxed, such a change is due to ML APIs’ updates.
Given a confusion matrix of the ML API measured previously (say, a few months ago), C o, the ML API shift is deﬁned as ∆C ≜C −C O.
In fact, as shown in Figure 2, API performance changes exceeding 1% occurred in about 33% of all (36) considered ML API-dataset combinations.

API shifts are orthogonal to distribution shifts: instead of attributing the performance shifts to data distribution changes, API shifts concern with ML APIs changes which changes its predictions on the same dataset.
For a data point x from some domain X, let ˆy(x) ∈[L] denote its predicted label on x, and y(x) be the true label.
The sample size is obtained when a 1% Frobenius norm error is achieved with probability 95%.
For both methods, we choose c to ensure a 1% error under 95% conﬁdence level.
L01.notes: The 'uncertainty score' σ² and the 1500 averaged runs concern MASA's random choice of which items to query, not repeat queries of the same API version, so no same-version spread is ever measured; the authors state confusion matrices are for classification only and other measures are needed for NLP/OCR. Published later as Chen, Zaharia & Zou, 'How did the model change? efficiently assessing machine learning API shifts', ICLR 2022 (cited as [34] in L02).

L02.title: HAPI: A Large-scale Longitudinal Dataset of Commercial ML API Predictions
L02.who: Chen, Jin, Eyuboglu, Ré, Zaharia & Zou

C4a.object: A longitudinal dataset (1,761,417 instances) of commercial ML API predictions and confidence scores on fixed benchmark datasets queried once per evaluation period from 2020 to 2022, summarised by prediction overlap, confidence movement, accuracy and group disparity between periods.
C4a.quote: Prediction overlap measures how often an ML API’s prediction on the same input remains the same at different evaluation periods.
C4a.reason: The same-weights floor and the interval are both missing: each item is queried once per period, no same-period repeat is taken to measure the API's own spread, the checklist reports error bars as N/A, and shifts are reported as raw prediction-overlap, confidence-movement and accuracy differences with no interval; the object is API-reported labels and confidence scores, not teacher-forced log-probabilities.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Chen et al. 2022 grade year-to-year prediction overlap and confidence movement against no floor and no interval

bearing_quotes: Prediction overlap measures how often an ML API’s prediction on the same input remains the same at different evaluation periods.
For a ﬁxed data point, an ML API’s prediction can remain the same, but its conﬁdence may still move up and down over time.
For each ML API and dataset pair, we recorded the API’s prediction f(x, t) and q(x, t) at each evaluation time.
Speciﬁcally, we have evaluated all classiﬁcation APIs in the spring of 2020, 2021, and 2022, separately, and all structured prediction APIs in 2020 fall and 2022 spring respectively.
(c) Did you report error bars (e.g., with respect to the random seed after running experiments multiple times)? [N/A]
Our analysis shows that API shifts are common: more than 60% of the 63 evaluated API-dataset pairs encounter performance shifts.
This indicates general phenomena in API shifts: many API updates ﬁx certain errors but also make additional mistakes.
Overall, this analysis suggests that signiﬁcant changes can happen within six months and thus frequent updates of the database is needed.
L02.notes: HAPI is nearer than L01 on the object axis because it records and compares API confidence scores q(x,t) across periods (a soft score, not a hard label), but it is a dataset paper with descriptive statistics only: one query per item per period, no repeat runs, no intervals. Same author group as L01; its [34] is L01's ICLR 2022 version, not a new lead.

L03.title: ChatLog: Recording and Analyzing ChatGPT Across Time

C4a.object: The gpt-3.5-turbo API's sampled responses over time (1000 fixed ELI5 questions sent three times daily from 2023-03-05; 38,730 fixed JAT benchmark questions monthly), scored by ROUGE, accuracy and F1, with successive periods compared by a z-test against the within-period day-to-day spread of scores.
C4a.quote: we conduct a statistical test that measures the degree of variation that can be attributed to version change rather than sampling randomness.
C4a.reason: It compares the served model with its own earlier self on a fixed item set and grades period-to-period change against an in-situ spread by z-test, but it reports z-scores against critical values with no interval on the comparison, the floor is a within-period temporal spread on a black box whose weights are inferred (not known) to be unchanged, and the object is ROUGE/F1 on temperature-1 sampled generations rather than teacher-forced log-probabilities.
C4a.nearer_reason: Unlike Thinking Machines 2025 (same-weights spread measured but not used to grade) or Dutta et al. 2024 (compression flips/KL, no floor), ChatLog compares the same served API with its earlier self on a fixed item set and grades the change against an in-situ spread with a significance test; it still lacks an interval and uses ROUGE/F1 on sampled generations rather than log-probabilities.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Tu et al. grade successive-period ROUGE means of gpt-3.5-turbo against within-period day-to-day spread by z-test

bearing_quotes: Although the default decoding parameter (temperature = 1) introduces randomness in responses, we mitigate this by sending the same set of 1000 questions to ChatGPT three times each day.
These 1000 questions have been repeatedly sent to ChatGPT from March 5 to now. There have been 207 days’ data recorded and evaluated until the paper submission.
Let P represent the language modeling probability of the changing black-box model, and t denote the time interval between every two evaluation with the same questions Q.
Let T1 and T2 denote two successive periods, if the model’s version is not changed from T2 to T1, then their average performance µ1, µ2 should be equal.

There are two significant version changes, one is in March 24 with a z-score of 16.98, another is in June 28 with a z-score of −142. Both of them are larger than the critical value 2.58 of z-score at the 99% confidence level.

For each stable version after March 24, we split their records into two evenly long parts, and the z-score of each part is −1.006 and 0.1629 respectively, which are smaller than the critical value 1.96 of z-score at the 95% confidence level. Therefore, we believe that ChatGPT are stable on these days.

Specifically, in the stable range after April, the curve of only one trail’s result exhibits relatively large fluctuations, but it doesn’t reach the level of difference observed between March and April due to version changes.
For evaluation on the generation task (Fan et al., 2019) of ChatLog-Daily, we choose the widely-used rouge (Lin, 2004) metric to measure the token-level overlap with the reference.
leads: Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, and James Zou. 2023. How is chatgpt’s behavior changing over time? arXiv preprint arXiv:2307.09009.
Rachith Aiyappa, Jisun An, Haewoon Kwak, and Yong-Yeol Ahn. 2023. Can we trust the evaluation on ChatGPT? arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.12767.
L03.notes: The extracted text is arXiv:2304.14106v2 (18 Jun 2024), retitled 'ChatLog: Carefully Evaluating the Evolution of ChatGPT Across Time', not the v1 title in the protocol list. The z-test (eq. 5) uses the standard deviation of daily rouge-1-p averages within each period as its floor, not the 3-trial same-day spread; the 3-trial spread is used only to average scores and for a visual comparison in Appendix A.2, and the paper never has access to weights, so 'same version' within a period is an inference from stability, not a measurement.

L04.title: A Fingerprint for Large Language Models

C4a.object: Ownership verification of a suspect LLM: whether its API logit or probability vectors lie in (or nearly span) the column space of the victim model's retained last linear layer, with a fixed numerical tolerance and no time series.
C4a.quote: We model the problem of fingerprint authentication as the task of evaluating the similarity between the space of the victim model and the space of the suspect model.
C4a.reason: It fingerprints a model to identify which model it is (provenance/ownership/derivative detection), the very class the protocol assigns to OCCUPIES; there is no comparison of a served model with its earlier or differently-served self on a fixed item set, no measured same-weights floor (the tolerance er is fixed to 1 a priori), and no interval on any comparison.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Yang & Wu grade suspect-model logit subspace distance against a fixed numerical tolerance for ownership

bearing_quotes: The defender, who retains access to their own model’s parameters, including the final linear layer as a fingerprint, aims to verify ownership by querying the suspect model through API access.
Let e represent the error tolerance induced by numerical instability. If d < e, we conclude that s is compatible with L, indicating that the suspect model is likely derived from the victim model.
For each experiment, we generate (or recover) 300 complete logits (or probabilities) for simulation. The error parameter er is fixed to 1 across all experiments.
It is worth to note that although this is the average results, this consistency will hold even with only a few samples in practice, thus also enabling rapid verification.

We also compare with a new version termed as Gemma-2, which shares the same structure but under a novel training method, leading to substantial income and completely different outputs for the identical inputs.

Overall, this research offers a practical and effective solution for LLM provenance tracking and ownership protection, and outlines a promising direction for future research on secure deployment of generative models.
By querying the model with the same prompt, the complete probabilities p can be perfectly reconstructed, according to the above operation.
leads: M. Finlayson, X. Ren, S. Swayamdipta. Logits of API-protected LLMs leak proprietary information. In: Proc. Conference on Language Model, 2024.
N. Carlini, D. Paleka, K. D. Dvijotham et al. Stealing part of a production language model. In: Proc. International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 5680-5705, 2024.
L04.notes: The extracted text is arXiv:2407.01235v2 dated 7 Dec 2025, a revision later than the 2024 date in the protocol list. The object is next-token logit/probability vectors used for subspace membership (logits s = Wz), not per-item teacher-forced scores; the prompts behind the 300 logits are not described as a fixed or hashed item set.

L05.title: Beyond Preserved Accuracy: Evaluating Loyalty and Robustness of BERT Compression

C4a.object: Compressed BERT students (post-training/QAT int8 quantization, head pruning, distillation, module replacing) compared with the original finetuned BERT teacher on the MNLI and SST-2 test sets by label loyalty (agreement rate) and probability loyalty (1 minus root JS divergence of predicted label distributions), reported as mean plus/minus std over 3 runs.
C4a.quote: For quantization and pruning, the source model is the same finetuned teacher.
C4a.reason: Post-training quantization and pruning of the same finetuned teacher are a differently-served self on a fixed item set, and 3-run plus/minus values are reported, but no same-weights or seed-to-seed floor is measured or used: the teacher's loyalty to itself is 100 by construction and no null spread of teacher-vs-teacher is ever computed, so the loyalty drop is never graded against a floor.
C4a.nearer_reason: Same practice as the pass-2 neighbour Dutta et al. 2024 (label flips = 1 - label loyalty; JS divergence beside KL under compression), three years earlier and with 3-run plus/minus, but equally without a floor; an earlier equivalent, not a nearer one.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Xu et al. grade compressed-BERT label and probability loyalty against the uncompressed teacher, without a floor

bearing_quotes: we propose two new metrics, label loyalty and probability loyalty that measure how closely a compressed model (i.e., student) mimics the original model (i.e., teacher).

Label loyalty directly reflects the resemblance of the labels predicted between the teacher and student models. It is calculated in the same way as accuracy, but between the student’s prediction and the teacher’s prediction, instead of ground labels:
As such it is desirable to have a metric to measure to what extent the “production model” is different from the “development model”.
Table 1: Accuracy, loyalty and robustness of compressed models on the test set of MNLI (3 runs).
Additionally, we directly optimize the KL divergence (i.e., pure KD loss) to set an upper bound for probability loyalty.
Also, we do not observe a significant difference between pretraining KD and downstream KD in terms of both loyalty and robustness (p > 0.1).
leads: Sara Hooker, Nyalleng Moorosi, Gregory Clark, Samy Bengio, and Emily Denton. 2020. Characterising bias in compressed models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.03058.
L05.notes: The plus/minus values are standard deviations over 3 runs of each compression/training, i.e. a spread on the student side, not a confidence interval on the teacher-student difference and not a floor; the only significance test (p > 0.1) is between two students, never against a null. The probability object is a 3-class label distribution per item (JS divergence), not token log-probabilities.

L06.title: What Do Compressed Deep Neural Networks Forget?

C4a.object: Populations of 30 independently trained ResNets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CelebA) pruned during training or quantized post-training, compared with the non-compressed population on the test set: per-class recall shift graded by Welch's t-test (p <= 0.05) across the populations, and Pruning Identified Exemplars defined by modal-label disagreement between populations.
C4a.quote: For each class c, we we use a two-tailed, independent Welch’s t-test (Welch, 1947) to determine whether the mean-shifted class accuracy Sc t = {βc t,k −βM t,k}K k=1 of the samples Sc t and Sc 0 differ significantly. If the p-value <= 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and consider the class to be disparately impacted by t level of compression relative to the baseline.
C4a.reason: It grades the compressed-vs-base comparison on a fixed item set against a measured null, but the null is a seed-to-seed floor (the spread across 30 independently trained models) rather than a same-weights floor measured under the serving in use; pruned models are separately trained rather than the same weights (only the post-training quantized models are a differently-served self), the object is hard predictions with probabilities explicitly avoided, and p-values are reported with no interval on the comparison.
C4a.nearer_reason: Its quantization arm applies post-training int8/float16 quantization to the same trained weights and grades the population shift against a measured seed-to-seed null with a significance test, which Dutta et al. 2024's flips/KL (no floor) lack; the floor is across seeds, not same-weights, and the object is labels, not log-probabilities.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Hooker et al. grade compressed-vs-base class recall against a 30-seed population null by Welch's t-test

bearing_quotes: We independently train a population of K models for each compression method, dataset, and model that we consider. Thus, we have a sample Sc t of accuracy metrics per class c at each level of compression t.

Our goal is to move beyond anecdotal observations, and to measure statistical deviations between populations of models. Thus, we report metrics and statistical signiﬁcance for each dataset, model and compression variant across 30 independent trainings.
For each level of pruning t, we train 30 models from random initialization.
All networks were trained with 32-bit ﬂoating point weights and quantized post-training. This means there is no additional gradient updates to the weights post-quantization.

Given the limitations of un-calibrated probabilities in deep neural networks (Guo et al., 2017; Kendall & Gal, 2017), we focus on the level of disagreement between the predictions of compressed and non-compressed networks on a given image.
The exemplar is classiﬁed as a pruning identiﬁed exemplar PIEt if and only if the modal label is different between the set of t-pruned models and the non-pruned baseline models:
Along with the p-value, for each class we report the average relative deviation in class-level accuracy, which we refer to as relative recall difference:
We note that there is no constraint that the non-pruned predictions for PIEs match the true label. Thus the detection of PIEs is an unsupervised protocol that can be performed at test time.
L06.notes: The extracted text is arXiv:1911.05248v3 (6 Sep 2021). The floor is the between-seed variance of 30 independent trainings per condition (Welch's t-test on mean-shifted class accuracy), which is a different null from a same-weights, same-serving floor; pruning is applied progressively over training so pruned and baseline populations never share weights, while the three quantization methods are applied post-training to the trained weights and so are differently-served selves of the same population.

L07.title: Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings

C4a.object: The run-to-run spread of accuracy and output strings of five served LLMs at temperature zero on eight fixed BBH/MMLU task subsets across ten identical runs, reported as a measurement of instability.
C4a.quote: Here we look at an additional source of uncertainty, performance variance from the same trained model on the same inputs when temperature=0.
C4a.reason: OCCUPIES: the same-weights in-situ spread is measured but never used as a floor to grade a comparison of the model with an earlier or differently-served self (the local-GPU Llama-3-8B run is an ungraded aside), no interval is put on any comparison, and the object is accuracy and output strings rather than log-probabilities.
C4a.nearer_reason: Same distance as Thinking Machines 2025: both measure a same-weights spread of served completions and neither grades a comparison against it; Atil et al. predate it (Aug 2024) and add only an ungraded local-GPU-versus-API contrast for Llama-3-8B.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Atil et al. measure output and accuracy spread across ten temperature-zero runs of five served LLMs

bearing_quotes: We investigate non-determinism in five LLMs configured to be deterministic when applied to eight common tasks in across 10 runs, in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.
We set the temperature at 0, top-p at 1, and fix the seed. We use the same compute infrastructure, inputs, and configurations.
Total agreement rate@N (TAR@N): the percentage of test set questions across N runs where generated answers are all identical, regardless of whether the answer was correct.
Note that we do not report standard deviations of means because the distributions across runs for a given condition are not normally distributed (see below).
Accuracy over 20 identical runs on college math, temperature=0, top-p=1. Median in blue, mean in black with dashed 5% and 95% quantiles.

In order to support this line of reasoning, we ran Llama3-8b on our local GPUs without any optimizations, yielding deterministic results. This indicates that the models and GPUs themselves are not the only source of non-determinism.

Additionally, we fine-tuned gpt-3.5 using two-fold cross validation. Although, the results indicate that fine-tuning helps reduce instability, we hypothesize that a fine tuned model cannot be shared across users and as such our tasks were the only ones being run.
We encourage reporting maximum-minimum scores across runs to have a more robust comparison of models.
leads: Yifan Song, Guoyin Wang, Sujian Li, and Bill Yuchen Lin. The good, the bad, and the greedy: Evaluation of LLMs should not ignore non-determinism. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.10457, 2024.

Shuyin Ouyang, Jie M. Zhang, Mark Harman, and Meng Wang. An empirical study of the non-determinism of ChatGPT in code generation. ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology, 34(2), January 2025.
L07.notes: Atil et al. measure the floor and nothing else: ten temperature-zero runs per condition on the same API, reported as TAR@10 and max-min accuracy spread with quantiles but no standard deviations and no interval on any comparison; the item set is fixed (eight task subsets, 100-282 items each) but not hashed. The local-GPU Llama-3-8B run and the gpt-3.5 fine-tune are asides in the Discussion, not graded comparisons; the two leads are the same nondeterminism-measurement class, not nearer.

L08.title: Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks

C4a.object: Variance of benchmark scores across ten Llama-2-7B models pretrained from scratch differing only in initialisation seed (210 checkpoints), across training checkpoints, and across 280 public models, on 13 fixed benchmarks, with bootstrapped and analytic 95% confidence intervals and continuous probability-mass / target-NLL metrics.
C4a.quote: to conclude that pretraining dataset or hyperparameter set B is better than pretraining dataset or hyperparameter set A, we would want the performance increase to be larger than that due to random seed variance across different models trained in setup A.
C4a.reason: The self-comparison and the same-weights floor are missing: the measured null floor is seed variance across different weights trained from different initialisations (and drift across training checkpoints), used to grade comparisons between training setups and evaluation methods, not a served model compared with its own earlier or differently-served self on the same weights under the serving in use.
C4a.nearer_reason: Nearer on the practice, not the object: of the four sources and the two pass-2 neighbours as described, it is the only one that both measures a null floor and states that a comparison must exceed it, with 95% intervals, on fixed item sets, using probability-mass / target-NLL (log-prob-level) scores; but its floor is seed variance across different weights and it compares training setups, so Thinking Machines 2025 remains nearer on the same-weights in-situ floor and Dutta 2024 on the differently-served self.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Madaan et al. grade benchmark score differences against measured seed variance and bootstrapped 95% intervals, on different weights

bearing_quotes: These 10 runs are identical, except for the model initialisation seed.

to conclude that pretraining dataset or hyperparameter set B is better than pretraining dataset or hyperparameter set A, we would want the performance increase to be larger than that due to random seed variance across different models trained in setup A.
To ground the seed variance numbers, we compare them with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals on individual models, as well as observed variance across different setups.

To maintain consistency, we used probability mass of the predicted answer for all choice-based benchmarks and NLL of the correct answer for generation-based benchmarks; more details are provided in Appendix A.
We observe that the SNR is considerably higher for continuous metrics for all benchmarks, suggesting that they may be better when comparing models in the sense that they are less confounded by noise.
Generally, the 7B seed variance is well below the 95% CI for the same benchmark, though the ratio of the two is quite variable.

However, both methods suffer from greatly increased seed variance (final two columns, Table 3), indicating that the tiny-benchmarks method may have limited use during pretraining ablations as it makes model comparisons more likely to be confounded by randomness from the initialisation and data ordering seed.
Despite this widespread usage, we rarely quantify the variance in our evaluation benchmarks, which dictates whether differences in performance are meaningful.
L08.notes: No served model, no serving-path variation, no repeat of the same weights: every source of variance measured is a different set of weights (seed) or a different checkpoint. Its finding that target-NLL / probability-mass metrics have higher SNR than discrete accuracy bears on the sand's choice of a log-prob object but does not occupy the served-self comparison.

L09.title: LLMmap: Fingerprinting For Large Language Models

C4a.object: Identification of which of 42 LLM versions an LLM-integrated application is serving, from generated-text responses to eight fixed crafted queries fed to a trained classifier or a signature database.
C4a.quote: We model an adversary A whose objective is to determine the exact version vi of the LLM deployed in remote application B with the minimal number of queries to O. We refer to this adversarial goal as “LLM fingerprinting”.
C4a.reason: OCCUPIES: the practice fingerprints a served model to identify which version it is (provenance); there is no comparison of a model with its own earlier or differently-served self, no same-weights floor, and no interval on such a comparison, the only standard deviations being over ten training runs of the classifier; the object is generated text, not log-probabilities.
C4a.nearer_reason: Provenance identification is a different object from both pass-2 neighbours; Appendix C's cosine distances between fine-tuned derivatives and their base model are derivative detection with no floor.
C4a.neighbour_phrase: Pasquini et al. identify which LLM version an application serves across 42 versions from eight fixed queries

bearing_quotes: LLMmap employs an active fingerprinting approach, sending carefully crafted queries to the application and analyzing the responses to identify the specific LLM version in use.
(2) Intra-model Consistency: A robust query should produce stable outputs even when the LLM is subjected to different prompting configurations or randomness.
However, it assumes access to the logits output generated by the LLM being tested, rather than the actual generated text.
After this optimization process, we finalized a query strategy composed of 8 highly effective queries, which are listed in Table G.2.
Accuracies and standard deviation computed on 10 models’ training runs.
Given those 5 models, we use the open-set LLMmap to derive a fingerprint signature for each variant and compare their vector signature with the vector signature of the base model.
However, we observed that the scale of the minimum distance often depended on the specific LLM under consideration, making it highly variable taken alone.
Fingerprinting a model q is then performed by finding the vector signature in the database DB that is closest to f(q).
leads: Mark Russinovich and Ahmed Salem. Hey, that’s my model! introducing chain & hash, an llm fingerprinting technique. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.10887, 2024.
L09.notes: A provenance tool for red teams: eight fixed text probes (banner grabbing, alignment refusals, malformed input, prompt-injection triggers) and an 8M-parameter classifier or cosine-matched signature database; the ±figures in Table 2 are over ten training runs of the classifier, and Appendix E's unseen-model detector thresholds distances between different models, not a same-weights spread. Yang & Wu (their [47], logit-based) is already L04 on the closed list; the Russinovich & Salem lead hashes responses to predefined queries but for ownership, so it is a mechanism echo, not a nearer object.

L10.title: Hide and Seek: Fingerprinting Large Language Models with Evolutionary Learning

C4a.object: Attribution of a black-box LLM to its model family (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Phi) by an Auditor LLM that evolves prompts across trials and a Detective LLM that picks the two same-source models out of a lineup.
C4a.quote: The Detective is informed that two of the models in the set are from the same "source" (either identical models or from the same model family). Its task is to identify these two models based on similarities in their outputs.

L12.title: Copy, Right? A Testing Framework for Copyright Protection of Deep Learning Models

C4a.object: Whether a suspect model is a stolen copy (finetuned, pruned or extracted) of a victim model, decided by voting over output- and activation-distance metrics on a generated test suite, each thresholded against independently trained negative models.

bearing_quotes: DEEPJUDGE quantitatively tests the similarities between two deep learning models: a victim model and a suspect model.

For each testing metric λ, we set the threshold adaptively using an ε-difference strategy. Speciﬁcally, we use one-tailed T-test to calculate the lower bound LBλ based on the statistics of the negative suspect models at the 99% conﬁdence level.

To supplement this evaluation, we tested the models with 500 composite numbers.
To generate composites, we randomly selected 500 products of two primes. We constrained them to be in the same numerical range as the primes in the authors’ data (1000 – 20000).
What seems to have changed is that the March version of GPT-4 almost always guesses that the number is prime, and the June version almost always guesses that it is composite.
In short, everything in the paper is consistent with the behavior of the models changing over time. None of it suggests a degradation in capability.
Given the nondeterministic nature of LLMs, it takes a lot of work to discover these strategies and arrive at a workflow that is well suited for a particular application.
